passage: The steel box of laddoos sat on the top shelf of the Pune flat. Chinmayi, five, had already eaten one after dinner. "One more, Papa!" Her father, Mridul, shook his head and closed the lid. Her face went red before she said a single word. Her feet stamped on the tiles, once, twice, hard. "I hate you!" she shouted, fists tight. "It's not fair! You always say no!" She threw herself onto the sofa cushion, kicking. Mridul stood still, the box in his hand, while the shouting filled the small room.

qa.q: Where was the box of laddoos kept?
qa.a: The steel box of laddoos sat on the top shelf of the Pune flat.

qa.q: What was Chinmayi feeling when her father closed the lid, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt it was deeply unfair and was furious 😠; her face went red and her feet stamped before any words came, then she shouted "It's not fair!"

qa.q: At this early moment, what could Mridul do that might help the evening turn toward calm?
qa.a: He could stay near her, name the anger in a quiet voice and keep the answer the same, so she learns that big feelings are safe but the limit holds.

qa.q: What is it like for Mridul to hear "I hate you" from his five-year-old?
qa.a: It probably stings even if he knows she doesn't mean it, and he may feel torn between comforting her and giving in just to stop the noise.

grounding: Shows a five-year-old girl refused a second sweet whose body erupts in stamping and shouting "I hate you" before calmer words come.

passage:
"Mumma, can I have another toffee?"
"You had one after lunch, Nandini. That's it for today."
"Just one small one!"
"No, sweetheart. The jar is closed now."
Nandini's chin wobbled. Her feet began to stamp on the floor, harder and harder.
"No! No! It's not fair!"
"I know you really wanted it."
"I hate you! I hate you, Mumma!"
Sunaina put the jar on top of the fridge and knelt down. "You're very cross."
"Go away!" Nandini shouted, stamping again, her cheeks wet and hot.

qa.q: Where did Sunaina put the jar?
qa.a: Sunaina put the jar on top of the fridge.

qa.q: Why did Nandini shout "I hate you" at her mother?
qa.a: She wanted the toffee badly and the no felt unfair; the anger hit her body first, so her feet stamped and the hurtful words burst out before calmer ones could.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Sunaina in this moment?
qa.a: She can keep the jar closed, stay close and name the anger calmly, which shows Nandini that the feeling is allowed but shouting will not change the answer.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel hearing "Go away!" right after she knelt down?
qa.a: She may feel pushed away and a little hurt, yet understand that Nandini is overwhelmed, so she might wait nearby rather than leave.

grounding: Illustrates a five-year-old girl denied a second sweet, stamping and shouting "I hate you" as her body reacts before reasoning.

passage:
"Amma, can I have another laddoo?" Ishita held up her sticky fingers.
"You had one after lunch, kanna. That's all for today."
"Just a tiny one! The box is full!"
"The box is for Nani's visit tomorrow. The answer is no."
Ishita's cheeks went red. Her feet started before her words did: stamp, stamp, stamp on the kitchen tiles.
"It's not fair! You always say no!"
"You really wanted it," Chandrika said.
"I hate you!" Ishita shouted, and threw her doll at the fridge.
Chandrika closed the box and knelt down, very still.

qa.q: What did Ishita ask Chandrika for?
qa.a: Another laddoo, even though she had one after lunch.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when her feet started stamping?
qa.a: She felt furious and that things were unfair; her red cheeks and stamping show the anger in her body before she had words for it.

qa.q: At this first stage, what could Chandrika do next that would help?
qa.a: Stay close and calm, name the anger for Ishita, keep the no, and make sure nobody gets hurt while the storm passes.

qa.q: What is it like for Chandrika to hear "I hate you" over a laddoo?
qa.a: It likely stings, even though she can see it is about the sweet, so she has to keep her own voice steady.

grounding: Shows a young girl refused a second sweet whose body reacts with stamping before she shouts "I hate you".

passage:
Note for Vasudha's family, Thursday
We had birthday sweets at club today, one each. When Vasudha asked for a second and I said no, before any words came she was stamping, fists tight, chin wobbling. Then a loud "I hate you!" and a kick at the table leg. I kept the plate out of reach, stayed beside her and said, "You really wanted another one." I moved the other children to the mat so she had space. She was quiet by story time but tired, so she may need an early night.
Thomas, club assistant

qa.q: Where did Thomas move the other children?
qa.a: To the mat, so Vasudha had space.

qa.q: What does Vasudha's stamping before any words suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt a rush of anger and unfairness that took over her body first; the feeling came faster than her words.

qa.q: Which of Thomas's choices helped most at this stage, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the plate out of reach while staying beside Vasudha and naming her wish, because the limit held without leaving her alone.

qa.q: How might Vasudha's family feel reading this note?
qa.a: Maybe a little embarrassed but reassured, because the note explains what happened calmly and tells them she may be tired.

grounding: Shows a young girl's body reacting with stamping and kicking, then shouting "I hate you", when a second sweet is refused.

passage:
The haat was loud with bells and frying oil. Nilesh bhaiya from next door had bought Farida one hot jalebi, and she had licked every sticky ring.
"Another one, bhaiya?"
"Your Ammi said only one. Come, the bus will leave."
Farida's lip shot out. Her sandals slapped the dust, harder and harder, until a goat looked up. "You're mean! I hate you!" she yelled, loud enough for the tea stall to hear.
Nilesh crouched beside her, holding the empty paper cone.

qa.q: Who bought Farida the jalebi?
qa.a: Nilesh bhaiya from next door bought her one hot jalebi.

qa.q: How can you tell that Farida felt angry before she said anything?
qa.a: Her lip shot out and her sandals slapped the dust harder and harder, showing she felt cross and hard done by before she yelled.

qa.q: What small step could Nilesh take while he crouches beside her?
qa.a: Keep his voice quiet, say he knows she wanted another, and still stick to what her Ammi said.

qa.q: What might Nilesh be going through when she yells in front of the tea stall?
qa.a: He may feel embarrassed with people watching and a little stung, while also worrying about missing the bus.

grounding: Shows a young girl refused a second sweet at a village market whose stamping comes before her shout of "I hate you".

passage: In their Nairobi flat, Wanjiru, who was five, finished her sweet and held out her hand for another. "No more today," Mama said, putting the tin on the high shelf. Wanjiru's face went hot. Her friend Selin, visiting, still had half of hers. "It's not fair!" Wanjiru stamped both feet so hard the cups rattled. "I hate you!" she shouted, then burst into tears and stamped again.

qa.q: Where did Mama put the tin?
qa.a: On the high shelf.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru feeling when she shouted 'I hate you'?
qa.a: She felt angry and that it was unfair, especially with Selin still eating, and her body reacted before her words could.

qa.q: What could Mama say next that keeps the limit?
qa.a: Something calm like, 'You're really angry. The answer is still no more today,' without shouting back or giving in.

qa.q: How might Selin feel watching this?
qa.a: Selin may feel awkward or a little scared, holding her half-eaten sweet while Wanjiru stamps and cries.

grounding: Shows a five-year-old refused a second sweet feeling it is unfair, her body reacting with stamping and 'I hate you' before words.
